analysis.one_liner: Lets employers discipline workers for "harassment or abuse" during union activity without it counting as unlawful retaliation.
analysis.headline: The bill went nowhere: introduced with one cosponsor, referred to the Senate labor committee the same day, and no hearing or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal labor law so that when an employer disciplines or fires a worker for "harassment or abuse" that happened during union-protected activity — a strike, picket, or organizing drive — that discipline is presumptively lawful. The National Labor Relations Board could still find retaliation, but only if its top prosecutor proves the worker was engaged in protected activity, the employer knew it, and the employer acted out of anti-union animus with evidence of a causal link, and even then the employer escapes if it proves it would have taken the same action anyway. The bill leaves "harassment or abuse" undefined.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers — especially companies facing strikes, picketing, or organizing drives — gain a stronger legal position: discipline labeled as punishment for "harassment or abuse" during union activity stands unless the Labor Board's prosecutor can prove anti-union animus with causal evidence and the employer cannot show it would have acted the same way regardless. Workers who are targets of abusive conduct by fellow picketers also benefit in the narrow sense that their employer can discipline the abuser without risking an unfair labor practice finding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers facing strikes and organizing drives

how_it_helps.text: Employers get a safe harbor: disciplining or firing a worker for conduct the employer calls 'harassment or abuse' during Section 7 activity (striking, picketing, organizing) is not an unfair labor practice unless the NLRB's General Counsel proves protected activity, employer knowledge, and animus backed by causal evidence, and the employer fails to prove it would have taken the same action anyway.

The stated purpose is shielding employees from harassment and abuse on the picket line: an employer can discipline a worker who abuses or harasses co-workers during protected union activity without that discipline being undone as an unfair labor practice.

analysis.who_pays: Workers who strike, picket, or organize. An employer could characterize heated or offensive conduct during a dispute as "harassment or abuse" and discipline them; the worker's only recourse is winning a Labor Board case in which the Board's prosecutor must prove anti-union animus with causal evidence, and the employer escapes by proving it would have disciplined the worker anyway. Remedies in these cases are typically reinstatement and back pay awarded years after the firing.

drawbacks.text: 'Harassment or abuse' is never defined in the bill, so an employer could apply the label to ordinary heated strike or picket-line conduct — loud arguments, name-calling — and discipline workers under its protection.

The bill raises the bar for proving retaliation: discipline is lawful unless the Labor Board's General Counsel establishes anti-union animus 'with evidence sufficient to establish a causal relationship,' and even a worker who clears that hurdle loses if the employer persuades the Board it would have taken the same action anyway.

The bill creates no new protection or remedy for employees who are actually targets of abuse; its only operative effect is to limit Labor Board review of employer discipline, so the harassment problem it names is addressed only indirectly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Abusive conduct on picket lines is a real problem, and letting employers address it is a legitimate goal. But the bill is a blunt instrument: it hands every employer a way to recharacterize discipline of strikers and organizers as punishment for undefined "harassment or abuse," and it makes the worker's remedy depend on a prosecutor proving a causal chain of anti-union animus. The gain for employers likely outweighs the narrow protection it offers to workers targeted by abusive picketers — and it is entirely hypothetical anyway, since the bill has not moved.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced and has sat there ever since — no hearing, no vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Sen. Tommy Tuberville introduced the bill on November 6, 2025, together with Sen. Bill Cassidy, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
The bill has one cosponsor, a Republican, and no other senators have signed on.
No committee action, hearing, or floor vote has been recorded since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Neither side has gained or lost ground: current Labor Board rules on disciplining workers during union activity stay exactly as they are, and the bill's backers have made no visible progress toward changing them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Neither side; the status quo held

for.name: Sen. Tommy Tuberville
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate labor committee.

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has been held; the only support on record is two Republican senators, with no Democratic cosponsor and no recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Employers facing strikes or union organizing (retail, logistics, manufacturing, hospitality)
industries.note: The bill gives these employers a legal shield to discipline or fire workers during union activity as long as the conduct can be called 'harassment or abuse,' which is left undefined. Their gain comes directly at the expense of the legal leverage workers rely on when they strike or organize.

Unions and organizing workers would find it harder to challenge retaliation, because discipline during protected activity is presumed lawful unless the Labor Board's prosecutor proves anti-union animus with causal evidence. Unions' interest here runs alongside the workers they represent.

analysis.trajectory: With two Republican sponsors, no hearing scheduled, and no cosponsors beyond one, the bill looks like most single-sponsor labor bills in a divided Senate: it will likely sit in the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee until the Congress ends in January 2027 without a vote.
